HEADLINE: Other passions
TEXT:
JACK HEATH Chief executive Philanthropy Australia Age: 60 Lives: Sydney

Youhave followedaTibetanBuddhistpractice since 1996after attendinganeventwith the Dalai Lama inSydney.Whatdoes it involve?

For one hour every morning and 30 minutes every evening I meditate in my attic. I sit on a pillow, cross-legged in a half-lotus position; good posture makes the mind clear. I wearwhatever is loose and comfortable.

What is the purpose of meditation?

As I see it, it’s to train the mind so as to be of the greatest possible benefit to all people and beings. If you see a picture ofme sitting inmeditation itmight look like I’ve mastered this thing, but if you could see insidemymind you’d know I have such a long, long way to go.

Whatpromptedyou to take it up?

For a number of years I’d had chronic fatigue butwas incredibly driven and busy. I was a speechwriter for PaulKeating in 1994 when our first childwas born sixweeks early. I was struggling to keep it together and at the end of the yearwent off to do a 10-day silent meditation retreat. During the retreat I realised that I needed to take care ofmyself, so I left my job. I didVipassanastyle meditation by a Burmese teacher for a year and did a number of 10-day retreats. I kept on coming across Tibetan Buddhism but I resisted it because it seemed to be a Hollywood bandwagon thing andmy pride didn’t want to be involved. I’d also become addicted to the meditation andwas more concerned about myself than others (including my family). That all changed after I attended theDalai Lama’s teaching.

You’ve been president of the Drogmi Buddhist Institute at TilbaTilba in southernNSWsince 2011. Howoftendoyouattend?

It’s a very special place nestled in the foothills of GulagaMountain looking out to Bermagui and the ocean wherewe have a wonderful temple made out of local timbers.

Wewould normally do three or four retreats each year, usually in the range of four to eight days.

Howdoyoufeel after your sessions? Energised and invigorated or relaxed and peaceful?

Some days I’m calm, other days energised, other days a bit disappointed at how undisciplined and unfocusedmy mind is.

Then I remindmyself that this is a long game, not to be impatient or overly ambitious.

Can you do different meditation styles to concentrate on different things?

Yes – how do I generate more compassion, how do I transform negative emotions including anger, howcan I bemore generous to others, to pray for people who are unwell physically andmentally or how do I simply calm down and arrest a racing mind? In essence, it’s all directed to the same things – to wish for the happiness of all beings, that they be free from suffering, and that they come to experience a deep-seated joy.

YoubecameCEOatPhilanthropyAustralia in January and want to introduce two weeks of “reflection leave” as you’ve successfully done at your previousworkplaces, ReachOut and Sane Australia. What is reflection leave?

It’s two weeks of paid leave separate to annual leave and if you don’t use it each year you lose it. Most people have something below the surface that they’d love to do. We get employees to come up with a proposal. Ideally it is a solo undertaking that is digital-free and involves conscious reflection. It might be exploring the family history or doing a hike. Then they come back and share the experience with the workplace.

Workplaces should be places of growth and fulfilment. Anecdotally I have no doubt the return on investment of 2 per cent of salary is huge. •

HEADLINE: Lost in headspace
TEXT:
Reading Matters

GLYN DAVIS Chief executive, Paul Ramsay Foundation

You’re an educator and amanager – and a writer.Who is the contemporarywriter you’d most like to be,most admire?

Hermione Lee’s newbiography of Tom Stoppard quotes another playwright saying he could not begrudge Stoppard’s good fortune. “It is actually one of Tom’s achievements that one envies himnothing, expect possibly his looks, his talent, his money and his luck.”

Canyoulist thebooks at yourbedside?

Alongside the Lee biography, like the rest of the world I’m reading LouiseGlück after her Nobel Prize. And Reset by Ross Garnaut,MarianWilkinson’s The Carbon Club and the new In TheNational Interest series.

You’reagreat admirer of Tennyson’s Ulysses.

Howdoes it speaktoyouat thismoment?

I’ve long admired Ulysses as a meditation on leadership and ageing – written by a man then 24 years old. I read it once at a reunion of Australian conscripts, including Vietnam veterans, andwas moved by the tears in the room. Beneath the Victorian sensibility, the poemevokes a longing to be back in the world, following the horizon like an arch through which gleams all still unknown.

Your latest book is On Life’s Lottery and it’s about breaking thecycleof generational poverty. Do the skills and cultural resources associated with the liberal arts, broadly defined, have a role to play here?

As the president of Infosys, Ravi Kumar, argued in 2019, when we invest in “liberal arts graduates, we gain people with human-centred skills”. Such graduates “approach problems in entirely newways”.

At the Paul Ramsay Foundation,we have chosen the widest possible array of skills – from anthropologists and political theorists to data scientists, lawyers, medical doctors and beyond.Knowledge is a team sport, innovation the outcome of intense conversations across the disciplines.

Doyou takemuchpleasure in rereading?

Both new and familiar. Rereading is often discovering a different book – who knew our understanding of the world shifts subtly over time? Since it proves impossible to keep upwith all newwriting, I have profound gratitude to reviewers and publications for welcome hints on new booksworth reading.

KLARA AND THE SUN Kazuo Ishiguro / Faber Thequestionofwhether robots have consciousness – or have thepotential to become conscious, given increasing levels of computational complexity – boils down toanuanceof definition: what precisely is consciousness? What makes us special?

The latest novelbyBritishnovelist andNobel laureateKazuo Ishiguro is a journey, infictional form, around this philosophicalproblem. It’s the storyof Klara, an “artificial friend” inhabitinga pale, sickly, dystopic future.What the reader experiences, in large part because Klara is the narrator, are the sensations and the emotions that make up her conscious life.

Klarahas a distinctlymeaningfulexperienceof theworld. Ishiguro’s subtle artistry is dedicatedto the convincingportrayalofher innerworldand her perceptions, withall their quirks and limitations.We learn early on that she is acutely observant,evenfor anandroid. “As you see, Klara has extraordinaryobservational ability. I’venever knownonelikeher,” says themanager of the storewhereKlara is displayedwhenwemeether.

Klara is solar-poweredbut deeply consciousof the sun’spower – his “special nutrition” – to the point of heliolatry. Just as humans have their deities, robots, in Ishiguro’sworld, have theirs.We learn that Klarahas a capacity fordeephuman connection, empathy, andultimately, selfsacrifice in the service of her human master. After oneparticularlybenevolent intervention,her interlocutor exclaims: “Oh, you darling robot!” This is a philosophical novel shorn of philosophical language,written in a stylenomore sophisticated thanaworkof young-adult fiction.

Much like Albert Camus’ The Stranger, it is spare, lapidary, a touch lugubrious. For a full appreciation of its boldness and novelty, it helps to get a handle on contemporary debates about artificial intelligence and consciousness.

Acclaimed American philosophers Daniel Dennett and John Searle take up sharply opposed positions in this debate;one thatwill come to defineour times as increasingamounts of human cognition are outsourced to algorithms. Dennett, fromTufts University, is amaterialist who argues it’s possible for robots to become conscious becausehumanconsciousness is “sorta” robotic.

“We’re robotsmade of robotsmade of robots.

We’re incredibly complex, trillionsofmoving parts. But they’re all non-miraculous robotic parts,” he says.Themind, inotherwords, is just a computerprogram; thebraina kindof hardware.

Searle, fromUCBerkeley, sees consciousness as a “biological” process – notamaterial one – and stresses its “private, subjective, qualitative” character. Consciousness is the result of “neurobiological”, not computational, processes.

Searle points out, rightly I think, that brains are distinctively human, distinctively biological.

Ishiguro takes a little of something fromboth sides of thedebateandarrives, throughthewhite magic of fiction, at an imaginative synthesis.With Dennett and the computational school, he presupposes that androids have thecapacity for consciousness and, inaccordwithSearle,he imagines howthat artificial consciousness might be felt and lived subjectively, and howitmight evolve. He asks us tobelieveinthepower of goodness – the power, ultimately, ofmiracles.

Thenovelwouldbemore consolingif, in addition to love and compassion, Ishiguro’s Klara alsohad a capacity for humour.The author’s fans will also notice the reappearance of tropes, such as thepsychologyof care andservice,braided into his earlier novels.

FROM THE BOOKSHELF CANDIDE Voltaire “Fools admire everything in an esteemed author,” offers the dyspeptic Venetian noble Pococurante in Voltaire’s fast-paced philosophical tale, Candide. EarlierPococurante, whose name in Italian means little (poco) caring (curante), takes down the esteemed Homer: “... one had to have it in one’s library, as a monument toantiquity, likethose rusty coins that cannot be put into circulation.”

In this masterpiece ofwit and invention, Voltaire,much likePococurantehimself, skewers human folly andpretensionwith zest andwithout pity.Madness iseverywhere. Cruelty, too. His main target is philosophical optimism, or the view that ours is “the best of all possibleworlds”.

Professor Pangloss,Candide’s tutor, is thebearer of this philosophy associated with the German polymathGottfriedvonLeibniz,but it has ancient precursors – particularly in the Greek Stoics.

This an adventure story, a freewheeling satire andanoften-bawdy romp. Theeponymous hero is a naïf: the illegitimate son of a German prince.

Candide’s sweetdisposition–not that he is immune tomelancholy – allows Voltaire to indulge his scabrous pessimism without tilting intototalmisanthropy. Therenever hasbeen agreement on themeaningof Candide’s closing imperative: “wemust cultivateourgarden.”And that’s as it shouldbe. Thenovella’smost enduring quality is not somuchits critiqueof Leibnizian optimism as its relentless and joyous satire.•

HEADLINE: QUARANTINE DREAM
TEXT:
A spoonful of caviar helps the vaccine go down, especially when administered by a private butler on a white-sand beach.

WHENSOMEMARKETING GURU came up years ago with the line “one island, one resort” to sell theMaldives as theworld’s most elite destination, they could never have guessed whatwas coming in the formofCOVID-19.

Even if maths isn’t your forte, the Maldives equation is blissfully simple during a pandemic: The tiny nation state (population 531,000) comprises almost 1200 coral islands (of which only 120 or so are private resorts) spread across almost 300 square kilometres, which basically equals plenty of space for everyone.

Almost all residents live on the main island ofMalé, site of the nation’s sole international airport, billed as “the gateway to paradise”. Beyond that, hotels confined to their designated islands have for decades floated in a solipsistic bubble. Coronavirus caused the nation to close its borders for 110 days, but since July 15 last year it’s been business as usual, albeit with precautions in place. Staff, for example, have been based on the island where theywork, reached only by speed boat or seaplane.Quarantine rarely boasted such white sand.

“It’s like we were tailor-made for these times,” reflects Indian-British hotelier Sonu Shivdasani, who put down roots in the Maldives more than 25 years ago when he moved fromLondon.He now owns three properties: Soneva Fushi, Soneva Jani and Soneva Kiri. Nightly rates range from $US873 ($1128) for two people in theMay toNovember low season to $US38,000 in peak periods for up to 12 people, including a private pool with water slide.

“Barefoot luxury is no longer the main selling point – it’s that you can hug people and stand beside them here with no fear,” Shivdasani says. “Our slogan used to be ‘no shoes, no news’; these days it’s ‘no shoes, no news, nomasks’.”

Once a pipe dreamfor most travellers – theMaldives boasts the highest concentration of luxury hotels in theworld with average nightly rates north of $US5000 for top villas – it is nowthe travel industry’s pandemic poster child.

Asmost nations watch tourismnosedive, theMaldives has held onto its designer flip-flop travellers despite losing its largest market, China, when that country closed its external border. TheMinistry of Tourism says itwelcomed 550,000 visitors from Europe, America and theMiddle East for the nine months it was open in 2020. And in February, an average of 3460 guests arrived per day.

“The world’s super-rich basically have nowhere else to go,” shrugs Nihat Ercan, JLL’s head of investment salesAsia-Pacific.

“TheMaldives continues to be pretty much the sole international beneficiary of that.”

In one of the strangest travel groupings of all time, theMaldives,Albania, Serbia and Tanzaniamade headlines last July for opening their borders to inbound travellers with no restrictions. By contrast,many European countries welcoming tourists banned the Britishwhen its rates spiked.

As Shivdasani points out, given that the Maldives’ economy depends on tourism and GDPwas plummeting – but infection rates had stabilised – it seemed foolish not to try.

Around this time, theWorld Bankwas predicting the Maldives would be one of the hardest-hit Asian nations in terms of economic destruction. “We knewwe Fiona Carruthers TRAVEL had the infrastructure and the skills to handle the situation,” Shivdasani says.

“When the pandemic hit, I had 70 guests across our three properties, and none of them wanted to return to their homes in Europe or wherever. They said right away that theMaldives was the safest place, and so they stayed fromMarch until July.”

Shivdasani pulled all-nighters to get his resorts COVID-ready, including flying in a fully kitted-out laboratory fromRoche in Switzerland for fast-turnaround testing. The proof is in the pudding. “We just had our busiest December-January period ever, far busier than 2019,” he says.

All travellers to theMaldives are required to produce a negative COVID-19 test taken 72 hours before their flight. On arrival in Malé, they’re flown by seaplane to their resortwithminimal contact. “Once our guests arrive, we perform a test right away; they’re confined to their villa for six hours or so, then free to enjoy the whole island after the test comes back negative,” Shivdasani says.

As for Ercan, he’s glad the early reopening has been successful and hopes more peoplewill consider theMaldives – only four hours from Singapore or Bangkok – as a family destination. “There are some very reasonable entry-level hotels like Mercure,Novotel andHoliday Inn, plus the Hard Rock Hotel, priced from $US250- $US350 a night,” he points out.

Ask Ercan if those properties come close to the $5000-a-night joints and he’s nicely philosophical: “Once you get there, the crystal-clearwater is all the same.”•

HEADLINE: Outpouring of ideas
TEXT:
An ‘Oscars of fine wine’ will open doors for new players in the wine industry.

GERARDBASSET,WHODIED IN 2019, was one of theUK’smost respected wine identities. He was one of only three people in the world to become bothaMaster ofWine andaMaster Sommelier; in 2011, he wasmade anOBE.

“Gerard’s legacy is not just about the awards and achievements,” says his friend Lewis Chester. “It’s about the fact that he mentored so many people who are now important in theworld of wine. That’s what hewas really known for: helping people and doing things that will make a difference.”

Chester, an investment manager and passionate wine collector, was one of the people whom Basset took under his wing.

They travelled to wine regions together; Basset encouragedChester to studywine and in 2014 they set up a company that, among other things, produces an annual fine wine report,which tracks trends and rates theworld’s top producers.

After Basset died,Chester started thinking about what he could do to honour his friend’s memory. “Then, about a year ago, I had this crazy idea,” he says. “Why don’t we take thewinners in our report and create the Oscars of finewine. Then I went toNina, Gerard’s widow, and I said,why don’t we raisemoney from the event and start a charity in his name?” The event, called theGoldenVines Awards, is scheduled for October at London’s exclusive Annabel’s Club. Two hundred guests will pay handsomely to drink 2005 Domaine de la Romanée Conti Grands Echezeaux and 1988 Chateau d’Yquem – poured from jeroboam, no less – and bid on dozens of exclusivewine and spirit experiences to raisemoney.

Thanks to extremely generous donations from wineries, support from leading producers around theworld (including the three reviewed here) and sponsorship from luxury brands, Chester thinks the event might make £2million ($3.5million).

When he started planning, Chester knew he wanted to use that money to effect meaningful change inwine. As Black Lives Matter gained momentum, forcing a reckoning in allwalks of life including the wine industry, his resolve was strengthened.

“Gerard would want us to do something thatwill have a major impact on the world,” says Chester. “And in the fine wine scene, there really isn’tmuch diversity at all. So I said to Nina I thought we should raise money for diversity and inclusion.

“Fine wine can be the engine that makes the money. Money solves all problems. Money opens doors. And open doors let more people in.”

The first initiative is two £50,000 scholarships for students fromblack and ethnic communities to undertake the Master ofWine orMaster Sommelier programs, including a £5000 travel bursary, internship and mentoring.

This is just the beginning. The Gerard Basset Foundation – Chester describes it as “the bank” – is also now seeking to fund diversity and inclusion initiatives worldwide, from working with established institutions such as the Wine and Spirit Education Trust to groups like the Africa Wine Club, which aims to get 200 students across Africa taking the trust’s exams each year.

InAustralia, discussions with a university are underway to fund an Indigenous scholarship on a winemaking course. And the Len Evans Foundation, the charitable armof the Len Evans Tutorial, an elite school for wine judges established 20 years ago by Australia’s ownmuch-loved wine identity, is looking atways to develop a similar Indigenous scholarship.

“I’mexcited,” says Tasmania-based wine educator Curly Haslam-Coates. “Becoming part of a strong network iswhere marginalised people can benefit.

And Golden Vines is offering solid money to provide good access to good people, not just crumbs from the top table.”

DOMAINE LAROCHE PETIT CHABLIS, 2019 Chablis, $40 Beautifully perfumedwithwhite flowers and hints of honey, this is fine, focused chablis, with the pulpy fruit of the chardonnay grape temperedby the chalkyminerality of the regional terroir. Imported by domainewineshippers.com.au TAYLOR’S 10 YEARS OLD TAWNY PORT Porto, $50 Different in style to a typical Australian tawny – it’s less sweet, with a little more finesse – this beautiful port has lovely spiced fruit aromas and an elegant, long,mellowoak finish.

vintagecellars.com.au NICOLAS CATENA ZAPATA 2013 Mendoza $162 Great example of a top redwine from Argentina that has benefited froma fewyears in thebottle. A blend of cabernet andmerlot, it has deep, complex flavours of rich currants and savoury leather.

Imported by negociants.com•

HEADLINE: FEEL GOOD FOOD
TEXT:
A new not-for-profit arts precinct in Adelaide has attracted some serious hospitality talent.

WILL YOUR FOOD TASTE better if the chef is being nice to the kitchen teaminstead of nasty? “Yes,” says BrendanWessels, former chef at d’Arenberg Cube in McLaren Vale.

It’swhy he leapt at the chance to head up Aurora, flagship restaurant of Light, Adelaide’s new not-for-profit centre for the creative arts.

“As a philanthropic organisation, Light has a mandate to be a very supportive, encouraging environment, as opposed to the draconian kitchen traditionally created by chefs,”Wessels says. “It has totally changed mymindset,my philosophy andmy life.”

The directive comes straight from the founders, Nick and SophieDunstone, who returned to Adelaide from London last year with a desire to build “aworking canvas” on which Adelaide-first live performances, music and visual arts could play out. So far, they have invested half of the estimated $20 million cost on the 1880s heritage-listed building and the immersive digital technology of its performance spaces.

When he’s not cooking kabayaki eel congee or skate with potato Dauphinois in Aurora,Wessels oversees Light’s Little Mission cafe and a “super-cool” laneway venue with a shipping container kitchen in which he cooks international street foods.

“I love that it’s all about approachable excellence and not $300 degustation menus,” he says. “We want people to come for great food and stay for a performance or a concert. We also want to show the people who work with us that hospitality can be a beautiful industry.”

auroraadl.com.au

GIN-CURED SALMON WITH SALMON SKIN CRISPS

DEGREE OF DIFFICULTY

SERVES 8-10

“This dish iswonderful for parties, with a glass of bubbles,” says Aurora chef BrendanWessels. “And the salmon-skin crisps are simple to make, yet so decadent.” His tip? “Ask your fishmonger for a couple of extra salmon skins – they oftenskinthe fishfor sale andhave them left over.”

Serve the salmon with blinis, bagels or hot, buttered toast, toppedwiththe caviar cream.

INGREDIENTS * 1sideoffreshsalmon, pin-boned and skin on * 300gseasalt * 150gcastorsugar * 150gmixedbotanicals(eg juniper, star anise, clove, citrus peel) * 150ml of your favourite gin * 1bunchoffreshdill * 60g sour cream * 25gsalmonroe(suchas YarraValleyBloody Shiraz Gin salmon roe) * Sea salt and freshly ground pepper to taste METHOD Soak the botanicals in the gin overnight, tossing occasionally.

Drain andblitz them in a blender to startbreakingthem down. Add a thirdof the salt andblitzuntil pulpy, thenmix with the remaining salt and sugar.

Place the salmon skin-side downon a tray andcoat the flesh with the curingmixture.

Refrigerate for 48hours.

Scrapeoff asmuchof the curemix as youcan, thenwipe off any excess. Finely chop the dill and spreadover the top.

Store in the fridgeuntil required.

Softenthe sour creamwith a rubber spatula and gently fold inthe salmon roe, sea salt and pepper.

Slice the salmon thinly on the diagonal andservewith the caviar creamand salmon skin crisps.

SALMON SKIN CRISPS * 3or 4 salmon skins * Oilfordeep-frying Use a pastry scraper toremove all flesh andfat fromthe skins.

Blanch each one for 30 seconds in really salty boilingwater and drain. Arrange on a baking tray linedwith baking paper (“be careful, the skin is very delicate,” warnsWessels) and bake at 80C until dry but still flexible, gently loosening the skins fromthepaper as they start to shrink. Cut the skins into serving-sized pieces. In a deep pan, heat the oil to 200C.

Dropthe skins inuntil they puff, thendrain andservewarm.•

HEADLINE: MUM’S THE WORD
TEXT:
INTHISWORLD, WHERETHE future is still maddeningly difficult to predict, it is my own champagne problem to prepare this column six weeks ahead of its print date. What to write when we have so little idea of what even the very near future holds? TheMet Gala, which ismeant to be held on the firstMonday inMay, has been rescheduled for September.What about Afterpay Australian FashionWeek, scheduled for the first week of June?Ask again later.

One thing I do know, though, is that it is time to buy your mother a present, and that you have about a week to do it.

Mothers hold a curious place in fashion. Rarely do we equate motherhoodwith style – the term “mumsy” dismisses the idea that mothers have any style at all (see also: “mum jeans”). Often it takes hindsight to see our own mothers for the chic women they are, and to understand that, whether your ownmotherwas particularly well-groomed or not, she will dictate theway you navigate your own appearance – well past childhood.

My mother taught me to spend well on good shoes and good underwear, and to take care of them accordingly. She steeredme clear of visible panty lines (VPLwas on a level of concern akin to Whitewater in the 1990s) and toward a proper alterationist.

We have different styles and like all daughters, I rebelled against hers. My mother wore mini-skirts well into her 30s,which appalledme at the time (now I look back and only see legs honed by daily cycling). She wears colour and patterns liberally; by contrast I dress relatively modestly, mainly in neutrals. I can only imaginewhat thismeans formy own daughters’ future wardrobes.

Perhaps the fact that motherhood is not seen as an especially stylish role is because it is only quite recently that mothers have had any place in fashion at all. Think of the great designers of the 20th century – Karl,Yves, Christian, John, Marc, Pierre, Gianni – allmen, all childless, designing for women whose lives looked nothing like their own.

That changed when Diane von Furstenberg andDonna Karan began designing in the 1970s. Both young mothers, they took a simple fabric – jersey – and separately, created new wardrobes forwomen.DVFmade an empire – and a fortune – fromherwrap dresses,which remain style staples today, and Karan debuted her Seven Easy Pieces collection. The range of simple outfit building blocks were intended to help working women get out the door – stylishly – eachmorning. The range – including a bodysuit, leggings, and a skirt, all in Karan’s signature black – was created in 1985 but looks as if it could have been designed yesterday.

Karan told a reporter at the time, “So many women find assembling the right clothes bewildering. They’ve discovered fastways to put food on the table, but they do not know howto get their wardrobes together easily.”One of Karan’s advertisements even showed the model RosemaryMcGrotha juggling a Filofax in one arm and a baby in the other. Karan may have been one of the first to do this but happily she is not the last – today there are somanyworking mothers in fashion it seems an injustice to name only a few. Victoria Beckham, StellaMcCartney and Tory Burch create stylish wardrobes for women who, like themselves, work and raise children. In Australia, Camilla Freeman-Topper of Camilla andMarc and RebeccaVallance fly this flag.

Our mothers are the first people who dress us; they are the original style influencers, the fashion editors who we just happen to be related to. They pull up our socks, quite literally, and yank down our hemlines. It is our mother’s voice we hearwhenwe take a coat with us as we leave the house.And if your mother is anything likemine, even in this unpredictable world, you can be sure that no matter what you’ve got on, she will say something about it.

HappyMother’s Day. •

HEADLINE: the eyes have it
TEXT:
When there’s the allure of a beautiful object at hand, time isn’t everything

IF THERE’SONEGROUP PAYINGWOMENTHE attention they deserve, it’s watch brands. From the venerable to the fashionable, the masters ofmeasuring time are unleashing their creativity – possibly as never before – in pursuit of the female wrist.

If thismakes sense, it’s a wonder it took so long. For decades, women’s watches were predominantly smaller versions of masculine pieces, petite or dressed up with diamonds or a mother-of-pearl dial. Then fashion brands entered the fraywith fun pieces, and women refused to be categorised, daring even to donmen’swatches – and carrying it off with style.

Meaning that a women’swatch today is, well, anything that appeals to a woman and furnishes her forearmwith something she finds beautiful to look at. For brands it’s not merely an opportunity to showtheir colours, there’s the growing commercial importance of the femalemarket.

Consider for a moment who buys upmarketwatches.

Around the world it’s professional people, their predilection for nice things and their ability to purchase themthat have driven the industry, a situationmirrored here.

InAustralia,women have entered the professions in increasing numbers; they’re a cashed-up market in their own right. No wonder brands are paying attention.

They’ve seen howmen view thewatch as a means of self-expression and require a whole selection of timers at their disposal. So the idea of well-remunerated women building a watchwardrobe is a tantalising opportunity not to be passed up.

This is leading to the design of timepieces for which time of day is merely a horological lead-in to a visual treat, and any complication is likely to have more to do with the jewel setting than, say, perpetual calendar adjustment.

Every brand seems to want in on this party. There’s Rolex, with heavenly hued dials; Hublot with spinning petal-like hourmarkers and cases in tinted sapphire; boy-brand Breitling with a South Sea capsule of colourful Chronomats just for her; andOmega with dainty new Seamaster Aqua Terras, while Bulgari finds ever-new ways to interpret the iconic Serpenti.

Moving in similar rarified territory, RichardMille has eschewed the usual carbon casing in a new version of the RM07-01 model – no romantic names here – which it uncharacteristically describes as “opulent”. Given it’s cased in white gold and paved entirely in diamonds we’d agree, although it’s theMille’s dramatic open-link bracelet rather than the usual strap, again set with round gems, that could be the killer reason to buy. Such a strap is no stranger to Chanel; this year it has created an electro version for its Premiere model shown here, which, apart from the colourful accents, remains unchanged.

Cartier has chosen a case shape from1912 to demonstrate itsway with colour, citing “intense research on pared-down simplicity” that led to the so-called Tortue model. Looking at the impressive result, one can only conclude there’s no place for such simplicity today. The Libre Tortue SnakeWatch is adornedwith serpent-like scale motifs, black and coral enamel accents contrasting with blue and grey shades, “brightened” by gold and 130 closed-set diamonds. Spanning 39mmby 31mm, the hand-wound watch is limited to 30 pieces.

Jaeger-LeCoultre has turned to its iconicReversomodel, making the most of the blank-canvas opportunities presented by its swivelling double-sided case. Shown is one of fourwatches inspired by the decorative jewels of the 1920s and “celebrating the poetry of flowers”. Why not.

Looking at them you don’t doubt the work required to produce suchminiature art pieces; first the engraving, then the enamellingwithmultiple coats over many days, and finally the inlays of wall-to-wall diamonds andmother-ofpearl, almost 100 hours of handwork itself. That said, the hero remains the hand-applied flora that wraps around the case fromback to bezel. The movement is hand-wound and just 10 pieces of eachwatch in the serieswill bemade.

For Chopard, ethical 18-caratwhite gold is the base for a new high-jewellery piece distinguished by a dial setwith five “dancing” diamonds and framed by a laurel wreath of marquise-cut precious stones set around the dial. There are three versions: diamond set, and supplementedwith blue or pink sapphires. Each features Chopard’s trademark five loose sparklers free-wheeling around the dial, adding to the animation.

And if your eye – andwallet – is drawn to something a little more demure? Chaumet has the delicate Joséphine Aigrettewatch, a white-gold teardrop of a thing measuring 27mmby 20mmwith a white engraved dial, dab of diamonds and a svelte satin bangle strap – happily available in a range of forearm sizes. Yes, themovement is quartz, but at just under $18,000 the saving is,well, looking good.

Which, if you’re a watch, is exactlywhere youwant to be. • BaniMcSpedden iswatcheditorof The Australian Financial Review.

HEADLINE: THE SHAPE OF THINGS TO COME
TEXT:
Brands are rediscovering women and women are rediscovering watches, with Dior the latest to bring something unique to the wrist.

EVERYNOWANDTHEN, ANDNOTTHATOFTEN, you see a watch that’s reminiscent of nothing you’ve seen before. More andmore, that watch is one intended for the femalewrist and emanates not from that usual crucible of the craft, Switzerland, but from an atelier associated with the finicky world of fashion. Chanel, Bulgari,Hermès and LouisVuitton have been showing us what a touch of tailoring will do for a timepiece.

Leading theway this year on the horological catwalk is Dior, with a collection that reimagines the very shape of a watch case.Not for this house of haute couture and jewellery anything as mundane as a round or square case, or even a combination of the two.

Rather, the seven watches in the GemDior (pronounced j’aimeDior, naturally) collection have a freer-form eightsided case,modelled after the natural formations of tourmaline. The strap is a bracelet or cuff, open at one end,

the shape of its links inspired by the tiny fabric swatches late founder ChristianDior pinned to his concept sketches.

While having the somewhat randomappearance of stratified layers of gemstones, the cuff is surprisingly wearable, easy to slip on at a moment’s notice, easy to slip off. (Not unlike Georg Jensen’s open-bangle watch designed by Swedish-born Vivianna Torun Bülow-Hübe in 1969, a trendsetter in its day.) GemDior is the brainchild (see opposite page) ofDior Joaillerie artistic director Victoire de Castellane, who describes it variously as “abstract-organic” and “a union between nature and couture”. It’s certainly daring and contemporary; de Castellane has also created 11 pieces of jewellery for the collection, including bracelets and rings with misaligned links.

The watch range is not only eye-catching; refreshingly, there’s a wide range of price points. Thatmeans you can pay $98,000 for the most colourfulGemDior watch, the one de Castellane herself wears, rendered in yellow gold with gemstones, its octagonal case set with turquoise and two carats of diamonds framing a malachite dial; or you can put a street-smart steel version with a blackmother-of-pearl dial on yourwrist for $7100. In between you can option things upwith lapis lazuli and tiger’s eye facings, and diamonds here and there. Themost expensive version comes in white gold paved with 625 diamonds, almost 10 carats’worth, for $155,000. Common to all, that angular 27mmby 25mm case, set-and-forget quartz movement and an additional strap in black calfskin or alligator – with water resistance to 30 metres.

All of whichmakes theGemDior, despite itswild-child form, a happily practical and flexible proposition, and, better still, one that couldn’t be mistaken for any other watch in your wardrobe.

HEADLINE: Maker of a masterpiece
TEXT:
FOR INTERNATIONALLY acclaimed, ParisbasedVictoire deCastellane, theGemDior range is but the latest feather ina storiedcap.

She came toprominence designingcostume jewellery forKarl Lagerfeld at Chanelbefore launchingDior’s fine jewellery division–which she heads–more than twodecades ago. Born into a French aristocratic family, de Castellane is renownedfor her creative feistiness and loveof colour and asymmetric forms. Herpersonal creations have beenpresentedatgalleries in LondonandNewYork. She spoke via video to watch editor BaniMcSpedden.

Is the creativeprocessofdesigningwatches very different to that for designing jewellery?

WhenI’mdesigningawatch, I always think that it’s a pieceof jewellery.The difference is onlybecause it’s showingthe time. Everybody today has this on theirmobile, so forme, what’s important is to create anobject, a very interesting object, that gives the time.

Doyou sitdownwithapadandpencil,ordo yougo straight to a computer?Howdoes it happen for you?

None of that! I have the idea inmy head, and I see it like a flash, and I imagine howI’mgoing to introduce it tomy team. Sometimes I make a little sketch, but it’s not like I am atmy desk and I’mdesigninglike that forone hour. It’s something very quick. I also usewords to explain exactlywhat Iwant. And then I’m following all the steps of the fabrication, of the development. But the idea is oneminute, then two years of fabrication.

Whatwas the idea behind the Gem Dior collection?

The inspiration came from nature, and also from couture. From nature, I sawthe shape, a very nice shape for the case. And the couture inspiration came fromlittle irregular samples of fabrics thatMonsieur Dior workedwith – that inspiredthe bracelets. I loved theywere not regular.

Was there amomentwhere you thought you would do a traditionalwatchband, orwas it alwaysgoing tobe this rather unusual configuration?

I startedwitha normal bracelet,but it has to be very original by itself, very special, and fit with this case. You have to think of the next step and the questionwaswhat happenswhen you do it in themetal.

Was this – and the shape of the case – a challenge for themakers given they’re used to producing something very symmetrical?

It’s always a challenge! Everything is a challenge butwe are used toworking with a very goodworkshop. Voila.We challenge them and we always find a way to do it well. It’s part of the complexity of theprocesswithpeople who are verypassionate. Forme, what is very importantwhen I’mdoing something asymmetrical is to find a balance, create a design that’swell-balanced.

Do you envisage the octagonal case being with us for a long time or is thismore of a seasonal range ofwatches?

No, no,no. It took toolongtomake it happen! Forme, it’s thebeginningof a classical Diorwatch [line].

For some people stones – malachite, onyx – have ameaning. Do they to you?

For some people, yes ... forme, not really.

What I love is only the emotion that I feel when I see stones, the colour, the design, and voila.

But I don’t imagine somethingmoreormagical.

When designing thewatches, who did you envisage them appealing to?

I don’t like to imagine them in categories. I prefer to imagine the watch only on peoplewho love it. Because forme jewellery or awatch has to be something you love and lovewearing. I think thatwhen you love something, youwear itwell.

Today, people aremuchmore ‘decomplexed’, a lot less shy than before.Men are really getting intowearing jewellery…evenpieces of jewellery thatwere really a symbol of feminism.

They don’tmind that side of the piece.

Willwe see an expansion of the Gem Dior range given the scope to accommodate differentmaterialswithin this format?

Exactly.What I love is finding somethingand developing it in a lot of different families. And, most importantly for me,making something good, creating something that I like for a long time.Maybe one time,we will do one in opal… an Australian homage.

(This shouldn’t entirely surprise. In the publication Dior Joaillerie: The A to Z of Victoire de Castellane released last year, de Castellane nominates the multicolouredmineraloid as her favourite, describing it as “every stone in one stone.” Perfect then for presenting in a petite octagonal frame – BMcS.)•
